desc:
You may change some characters of the lowercase string s to any other lowercase letters. After the changes, the string must be cut into exactly k non-empty consecutive pieces, each of which is a palindrome.

Return the minimum number of characters that have to be changed.

For example, s = "abc", k = 2 gives 1 (change c to b and cut a|bb), and s = "aabbc", k = 3 gives 0 (aa|bb|c).
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: First solve a simpler question: how many characters must change to turn one fixed piece s[i..j] into a palindrome? Think of mirrored pairs.
Backtracking would try every way to choose k - 1 cut points, which is far too many for n = 100, but the subproblems repeat: the best way to split a prefix into p pieces is reused many times.

Let cost[i][j] be the changes to make s[i..j] a palindrome, and dp[p][j] the best cost of splitting the first j + 1 characters into p pieces. The last piece starts at some i: dp[p][j] = min over i of dp[p-1][i-1] + cost[i][j].
editorial: A piece is a palindrome when each character equals its mirror partner. Making s[i..j] a palindrome costs one change for every mirrored pair that differs, so cost[i][j] = cost[i+1][j-1] + (s[i] != s[j]), with the cost of empty and single-character ranges being 0. The table is built for all pairs in O(n2).

Choose the cut points by dynamic programming (a memoised version of the backtracking search over cuts). Let dp[p][j] be the minimum cost to split s[0..j] into exactly p palindromic pieces. For p = 1 it is cost[0][j]. For larger p, try every start i of the last piece with i ≥ p - 1: dp[p][j] = min(dp[p-1][i-1] + cost[i][j]). The answer is dp[k][n-1].
Overall O(n<sup>2</sup> + k · n<sup>2</sup>), which is about 170,000 transitions for n = 100 because both the piece count and the ranges shrink.
